title: Introduction to Machine Learning
text:
The course presents mathematically well-founded techniques for analysing patterns and learning from data, rather than trying to mimic biological brains. Pattern recognition (engineering origin) and machine learning (CS origin) are essentially the same field: automatic discovery of regularities in data. The course is self-contained but math-heavy (probability, calculus, linear algebra). MATLAB is the required programming environment. Grading emphasises assignments, quizzes, mid-term and final; worst quiz and assignment scores are dropped.
Key concepts: Pattern recognition / ML is automatic discovery of regularities in data so that new examples can be handled. Biological brains are stunning pattern recognisers but their exact workings are still poorly understood; practical ML techniques give machines the appearance of intelligence.
Exam focus: Difference between biological intelligence and statistical pattern recognition / ML. Course goals and mathematical prerequisites.
Practical notes: Familiarise yourself with MATLAB early (vectorisation, array manipulation).

title: Curve Fitting and Regularisation
text:
Given noisy observations (x_i, t_i) the goal is to recover the underlying regular function that generated the data. A polynomial model y(x,w) = sum_{j=0}^M w_j x^j is linear in the parameters w even though non-linear in x. Least-squares fitting of high-order polynomials leads to over-fitting: the curve passes through every training point but oscillates wildly and generalises poorly. Root-mean-square (RMS) error on a held-out test set reveals the optimal model order. Regularisation (or Bayesian priors) can control complexity without explicitly limiting M.
Key concepts: Real-world data equals underlying regularity plus noise. Over-fitting means large coefficients, perfect training fit, poor test performance. Model selection via test-set / validation error or regularisation strength.
Formulas: y(x,w) = sum_{j=0}^M w_j x^j (polynomial of order M). E(w) = 1/2 sum_n (y(x_n,w) - t_n)^2 (sum-of-squares error). E_RMS = sqrt(2E(w*)/N) (root-mean-square error).
Practical notes: Generate synthetic data with sin(2πx) + Gaussian noise to study over-fitting. Watch the magnitude of the learned coefficients as M increases.
Exam focus: Why higher-order polynomials can be worse; role of regularisation / model selection.

title: Probability Theory
text:
Uncertainty arises from noise and finite data; probability theory quantifies it. The frequentist definition is the long-run relative frequency of an event. The lecture introduces the product and sum rules, conditional probability and Bayes theorem through simple examples (coloured boxes containing fruits). These rules become the foundation for all later probabilistic models.
Key concepts: Uncertainty sources are measurement noise and finite sample size. Bayes theorem relates posterior, likelihood and prior.
Formulas: P(event) = lim (N→∞) (#successes / N).
Exam focus: Product rule, sum rule, Bayes theorem and their interpretation.

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (Probabilistic Curve Fitting)
text:
Under the assumption that targets are generated by a deterministic function plus additive Gaussian noise, maximising the likelihood of the observed targets is equivalent to minimising the sum-of-squares error. The Gaussian is the queen of distributions because it appears so frequently in nature; its multivariate form is fully characterised by mean vector and covariance matrix.
Key concepts: Likelihood function p(t|x,w,β); ML estimate maximises it. Equivalence of Gaussian noise assumption and least-squares.
Formulas: N(x|μ,σ²) = (1/√(2πσ²)) exp{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}. Multivariate: N(x|μ,Σ) = (1/√((2π)^D |Σ|)) exp{−½(x−μ)^T Σ^{-1}(x−μ)}. β = 1/σ² (precision).
Exam focus: Derivation that ML under Gaussian noise recovers least-squares; meaning of precision.

title: Maximum A-Posteriori Estimation (Bayesian Curve Fitting)
text:
Placing a Gaussian prior on the weights and maximising the posterior (MAP) yields exactly the same objective as regularised least-squares. The regularisation coefficient λ is the ratio of the prior precision α to the noise precision β. Thus regularisation has a clear Bayesian interpretation.
Key concepts: Posterior proportional to likelihood times prior; MAP maximises the posterior. Zero-mean isotropic Gaussian prior on w recovers L2 regularisation.
Formulas: p(w|α) = N(w|0, α^{-1}I). −ln p(w|x,t,α,β) = (β/2)∑(y(x_n,w)−t_n)² + (α/2)w^T w  (λ = α/β).
Exam focus: Equivalence of MAP with Gaussian prior and regularised least-squares.

title: Optimisation and Model Selection
text:
Hyper-parameters (polynomial order M, regularisation strength λ, …) control model complexity and must be chosen carefully. S-fold cross-validation is a standard practical method but multiplies computational cost. The lecture also introduces the calculus of variations and Lagrange multipliers as tools for constrained optimisation that appear later in the course.
Key concepts: Hyper-parameters determine model complexity; model selection finds their best values. Cross-validation averages performance over multiple train/validation splits.
Algorithms: S-fold CV: partition data into S folds; for each fold train on S−1, validate on the held-out fold; average the S validation scores.
Practical notes: Cost of CV grows as S^k for k hyper-parameters.
Exam focus: Purpose and cost of cross-validation; role of Lagrange multipliers.

title: Decision Theory
text:
Once the joint distribution p(x,t) has been inferred, a decision must still be made. Decision theory tells us how to choose the optimal action that minimises expected loss (or misclassification rate). The lecture contrasts the generative approach (model p(x,t) then apply Bayes), the discriminative approach (model p(t|x) directly) and the pure discriminant-function approach.
Key concepts: Inference vs decision; minimum-error and minimum-risk decisions. Generative vs discriminative vs discriminant-function classifiers.
Exam focus: When to use each of the three modelling styles; definition of expected loss.

title: Information Theory
text:
Information content of an event is proportional to the surprise it causes, i.e. −log p(x). For independent events the information is additive, which forces the logarithmic definition. Entropy is the average information; Kullback–Leibler divergence measures the extra information needed when using an approximate distribution q instead of the true p.
Key concepts: Information h(x) = −log p(x) (bits or nats). Entropy equals expected information; KL divergence as relative entropy.
Formulas: h(x) = −log p(x). h(x,y) = h(x)+h(y) when independent.
Exam focus: Derivation that information must be logarithmic; interpretation of KL.

title: Parametric Density Estimation
text:
Density estimation tries to recover the unknown distribution p(x) that generated a finite sample. Parametric methods assume a functional form controlled by a finite parameter vector θ and then estimate θ (usually by ML). The approach is ill-posed in principle because infinitely many densities are consistent with any finite sample; model selection is therefore essential.
Key concepts: Ill-posed nature of density estimation; parametric assumption reduces the problem to parameter estimation.
Exam focus: Why density estimation is ill-posed and how parametric assumptions help.

title: The Gaussian Distribution
text:
The multivariate Gaussian is completely characterised by its mean and covariance matrix. Iso-contours of constant density are ellipsoids whose shape is determined by the Mahalanobis distance. A single Gaussian is intrinsically uni-modal; multi-modal data therefore require mixtures.
Key concepts: Mahalanobis distance (x−μ)^T Σ^{-1}(x−μ) defines the geometry of the Gaussian. Uni-modality limitation.
Formulas: N(x|μ,Σ) = 1/√((2π)^D |Σ|) exp{−½ (x−μ)^T Σ^{-1}(x−μ)}. d(x)^2 = (x−μ)^T Σ^{-1}(x−μ).
Exam focus: Meaning of the Mahalanobis distance and the role of the covariance matrix.

title: Non-Parametric Density Estimation
text:
When a parametric form is too restrictive, non-parametric methods estimate density locally from the data. Histograms partition space into bins and normalise counts by bin volume and total sample size. Kernel density estimators place a smooth kernel at every data point; k-nearest-neighbour methods adapt the volume so that exactly k points fall inside. All three methods trade bias against variance through a bandwidth / neighbourhood size parameter.
Key concepts: Histogram estimator p_i = n_i / (N Δ_i). Kernel and k-NN estimators as local density estimators.
Formulas: p_i = n_i / (N Δ_i).
Practical notes: Choice of bin width / bandwidth is critical; too small yields noisy estimates, too large oversmooths.
Exam focus: Bias-variance trade-off controlled by the smoothing parameter.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Regression predicts continuous targets. The simplest model is linear in both the parameters and the input features (including a bias term). Training consists of finding the optimal weight vector w* that minimises a suitable loss (usually squared error) on the observed pairs {(x_n,t_n)}.
Key concepts: y(x,w) = w^T x (or w^T φ(x) after basis expansion). Bias parameter absorbs a constant offset.
Formulas: y(x,w) = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + … + w_D x_D.
Exam focus: Distinction between linear-in-parameters and linear-in-inputs models.

title: Linear Classification
text:
Classification assigns an input to one of K discrete classes. Decision regions are separated by decision boundaries. Convenient target encodings are 0/1 for binary problems and 1-of-K (one-hot) for multi-class problems. Training finds the optimal decision surfaces from labelled data.
Key concepts: Decision regions and decision boundaries / surfaces. 0/1 coding (binary) and 1-of-K coding (multi-class).
Exam focus: Target coding schemes and the geometric meaning of a linear decision boundary.

title: Probabilistic Models for Linear Classification
text:
Three families of linear classifiers exist: discriminant functions, generative models (model class-conditional densities and priors then apply Bayes) and discriminative models (model the posterior p(C_k|x) directly). Logistic regression is the canonical discriminative model; its parameters can be found by iterative re-weighted least squares (IRLS). Generative models become impractical in high dimensions because they require many parameters and accurate density estimates.
Key concepts: Discriminant vs generative vs discriminative approaches. Logistic sigmoid turns a linear function into a probability.
Formulas: p(C_1|φ) = σ(w^T φ) (binary logistic).
Algorithms: IRLS for logistic regression.
Practical notes: Homogenise inputs (append 1) so bias is absorbed into w. Use the MATLAB \ operator, never inv(), for the weighted least-squares solve. driver_binary.m shows how to extract the first two MNIST classes and call train_lr / test_lr.
Exam focus: Why generative models struggle in high dimensions; derivation / intuition of IRLS.

title: K-means Clustering
text:
K-means partitions data into K clusters by minimising the sum of squared distances between points and their assigned cluster centres. It alternates between assignment of points to the nearest centre and recomputation of centres as the mean of assigned points. The algorithm is a hard-assignment special case of the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixtures.
Key concepts: Objective J = ∑_n ∑_k r_nk ||x_n − μ_k||² with 1-of-K indicators r_nk. Alternating minimisation over assignments and centres.
Formulas: J({μ_k},{r_nk}) = ∑_n ∑_k r_nk ||x_n − μ_k||².
Algorithms: 1. Initialise cluster centres μ_k. 2. Assign each point to nearest centre (update r_nk). 3. Recompute each centre as the mean of its assigned points. 4. Repeat until convergence.
Exam focus: Objective function and the two alternating steps; link to EM.

title: Gaussian Mixture Models
text:
A Gaussian mixture is a linear superposition of K Gaussians whose mixing coefficients π_k form a discrete distribution. Introducing a discrete latent variable z that indicates which component generated each observation yields the same mixture density and opens the door to the EM algorithm for maximum-likelihood parameter estimation.
Key concepts: p(x) = ∑_k π_k N(x|μ_k,Σ_k) with 0≤π_k≤1, ∑π_k=1. Latent-variable representation turns the mixture into a complete-data model.
Formulas: p(x) = ∑_k π_k N(x|μ_k,Σ_k). p(z) = ∏_k π_k^{z_k} (1-of-K).
Exam focus: Latent-variable derivation of the mixture; constraints on the mixing weights.

title: The EM Algorithm
text:
When latent variables make the observed-data log-likelihood intractable (the log is outside a sum), EM maximises a lower bound. In the E-step the posterior over the latents is computed with the current parameters; in the M-step the expected complete-data log-likelihood is maximised with respect to the parameters. Each iteration is guaranteed not to decrease the observed-data likelihood. MAP estimation is obtained by simply adding the log-prior to the M-step objective; a partial M-step yields the Generalised EM algorithm.
Key concepts: Complete vs incomplete data; expected complete-data log-likelihood Q(θ,θ_old). Monotonic improvement of the observed likelihood.
Formulas: Q(θ,θ_old) = ∑_Z p(Z|X,θ_old) ln p(X,Z|θ).
Algorithms: 1. Initialise θ_old. 2. E-step: evaluate p(Z|X,θ_old). 3. M-step: θ_new = arg max_θ Q(θ,θ_old). 4. If not converged set θ_old ← θ_new and go to 2.
Practical notes: For MAP replace the M-step objective by Q + ln p(θ).
Exam focus: Why the log-sum prevents direct ML; the two EM steps and the guarantee of non-decreasing likelihood.

title: Principal Component Analysis
text:
PCA finds an orthogonal linear projection onto a lower-dimensional subspace that either maximises the variance of the projected data or minimises the average reconstruction (projection) cost. Both criteria lead to the same solution: the leading eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix. PCA is widely used for visualisation, compression and feature extraction.
Key concepts: Two equivalent definitions: max projected variance / min reconstruction error. Principal subspace spanned by the top eigenvectors of the covariance.
Algorithms: 1. Centre the data. 2. Compute the covariance matrix. 3. Find its eigenvectors and eigenvalues. 4. Project onto the subspace spanned by the top-M eigenvectors.
Exam focus: Equivalence of the two optimisation criteria; geometric interpretation.

title: Neural Networks and Back-propagation
text:
Multi-layer neural networks can represent highly non-linear mappings. Training is performed by gradient-based optimisation; the required gradients are obtained efficiently by the back-propagation algorithm (chain rule applied layer by layer). The lecture also sets two programming assignments: IRLS for binary logistic regression and SGD for multi-class logistic regression on MNIST.
Key concepts: Neuron as a linear combination followed by a non-linearity. Back-propagation computes exact gradients via the chain rule.
Algorithms: Forward pass → loss → backward pass (local gradients × upstream gradient) → parameter update.
Practical notes: Assignment 1: implement generic IRLS, train on first two MNIST classes, report accuracy and confusion matrix. Assignment 2: implement SGD multi-class logistic regression on full MNIST. Tips: homogenise inputs, avoid inv(), use spdiags if memory is tight. driver_binary.m illustrates the binary MNIST subset extraction.
Exam focus: Computational graph view of back-prop; practical tips for logistic-regression assignments.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Hand-written digits (and many other visual objects) are invariant to translation, small rotations, scaling and elastic deformations. A fully-connected network can in principle learn these invariances but needs a huge number of examples. Convolutional layers exploit local receptive fields and weight sharing to build translation-equivariant feature detectors far more efficiently; subsequent pooling layers add a degree of invariance.
Key concepts: Neuron as a detector: fires when the input resembles its weight pattern. Local connectivity plus weight sharing yields convolutional filters. Pooling for approximate invariance.
Practical notes: The CNN assignment carries double weight and is not dropped.
Exam focus: Why weight sharing and local connectivity help with visual invariances.

title: Autoencoders
text:
An autoassociative network is trained to reconstruct its own input. When the hidden layer is narrower than the input (bottleneck), the network performs non-linear dimensionality reduction and is called an autoencoder. Autoencoders serve as building blocks for deeper architectures because they can be trained layer-wise in an unsupervised fashion.
Key concepts: Target equals input implies unsupervised learning of a compressed representation. Bottleneck forces the network to discover the most salient features.
Exam focus: Role of the bottleneck; why autoencoders enable deep learning.

title: Support Vector Machines
text:
SVMs construct a maximum-margin linear discriminant for binary classification. The optimisation problem is convex, guaranteeing a global optimum. The dual formulation depends only on inner products, which can be replaced by a kernel function (kernel trick) to obtain non-linear decision boundaries in the original space. SVMs do not produce posterior probabilities.
Key concepts: Maximum-margin hyperplane; support vectors alone determine the solution. Kernel trick: replace φ(x)^T φ(x') by k(x,x').
Formulas: y(x) = w^T φ(x) + b ; decision by sign(y(x)).
Exam focus: Convexity, support vectors, and the kernel trick.

title: Boosting and Committee Methods
text:
A committee of models often outperforms any single model. Bagging trains models on bootstrap samples and averages their predictions. Boosting (AdaBoost) sequentially trains weak learners, each time re-weighting the training set so that previously misclassified examples receive higher weight; the final classifier is a weighted vote of the weak learners.
Key concepts: Committee / ensemble is average or vote of several models. Bagging equals bootstrap aggregation; Boosting equals sequential re-weighting.
Formulas: y_COM(x) = (1/M) ∑_m y_m(x).
Exam focus: Difference between bagging and boosting; why re-weighting helps.

title: Conditional Mixture Models
text:
Unconditional mixtures model p(x). Conditional mixtures model p(t|x) by combining simpler conditional models (linear regression or logistic regression experts) whose mixing coefficients may also depend on x. Parameter estimation is again performed by the EM algorithm. The resulting models are known as mixtures of experts.
Key concepts: Mixture of linear regressions / logistic regressions for multi-modal conditional distributions. EM still applies because of the latent component indicator.
Exam focus: Distinction between unconditional and conditional mixtures; role of EM.

title: Mixture Density Networks
text:
Many practical regression problems (especially inverse problems) have multi-modal conditional distributions p(t|x). A standard neural network trained with squared error can only represent the conditional mean and therefore fails. A Mixture Density Network outputs the parameters of a Gaussian mixture (means, variances and mixing coefficients) that can capture arbitrary conditional densities.
Key concepts: Forward problems are often uni-modal; inverse problems are frequently multi-modal. MDN equals a neural net whose outputs parameterise a mixture density.
Exam focus: Why squared-error networks fail on multi-modal targets; what an MDN outputs.

title: Spectral Clustering
text:
K-means assumes clusters are compact and roughly spherical (centroid-based). Spectral clustering can find elongated or non-convex clusters by first constructing a similarity graph, forming its Laplacian matrix, and embedding the data into a low-dimensional space spanned by the leading eigenvectors of the Laplacian; ordinary K-means is then run in that embedding. The method therefore projects the data so that the desired clusters become more apparent.
Key concepts: Similarity graph G=(V,E) with edge weights s_ij; degree d_i = ∑_j s_ij. Graph Laplacian; spectral embedding followed by K-means.
Formulas: d_i = ∑_{j∈V} s_ij.
Algorithms: 1. Build similarity graph / affinity matrix. 2. Compute the graph Laplacian. 3. Find the first k eigenvectors. 4. Embed points into R^k using those eigenvectors. 5. Run K-means in the embedding space.
Exam focus: Why spectral embedding helps non-convex clusters; role of the Laplacian.
